catalog_quote: Stress is penultimate. Syllabic nasals may carry this penultimate stress. In some Arabic loans, stress is antepenultimate. (Ashton 1947:5)
sweep_summary: Swahili (swah1253) is in the catalog as fixed-strict penultimate (Ashton 1947:5). Of 13 works with stress in the title (12 distinct works; Kelly 1989 is duplicated), two were obtained and read: Vitale 1982 (SAL 13(3), open PDF downloaded from journals.flvc.org) gives a dedicated statement that stress is penultimate with pre-penultimate stress only in Arabic/Persian loans, largely as stylistic variation — refines the catalog's classification without changing it; Greenberg 1947 (JAOS 67, read from the archive.org scanned of the issue) is about verse metrics but states that Swahili words are invariably accented on the penult with accompanying length — confirms. Philippson's 1991 thesis abstract (theses.fr) calls Swahili a demarcative penultimate-stress system — confirms. Not obtainable: Temu 1984 (De Gruyter DOI 10.1515/9783110884685-080, paywalled; high priority), Mpiranya 1995 (Köppe book; high), Park 2000 (confirmed in MITWPL 36, print only; medium — its noise_flag is wrong), Brauner 1990 (STUF, paywalled DOI; medium, compound stress), Kelly 1989 (print; low), and the three 'Swahili prosody' papers in the journal Swahili (Meeussen 1967, Allen 1967, Hichens 1962/63; no online copy; probably versification, unconfirmed). Goodman 1967 concerns Bravanese (Chimwiini), a different variety.org, theses.fr and publisher/journal sites directly.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Swahili is typically penultimate; the only examples of non-penultimate stress are found in loanwords usually of Arabic or Persian origin. Even if the stress of the original form were penultimate, it often shifts due to the breaking up of certain non-Bantu consonant clusters within the form by the historical addition of epenthetic vowels or the addition of a final vowel to maintain the canonical form of the open syllable. In some of these forms, there is variation between penultimate and non-penultimate stress due to the different degrees of assimilation. [...] There are very few minimal pairs which demonstrate contrastive stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog (fixed penultimate, non-contrastive) and as Vitale 1982 / Polomé 1967 / Steere held by the project; confirms from the thesis body what the earlier abstract-only reading reported (demarcative penultimate accent). It adds a dialect-scope qualification (most Swahili dialects; Mwiini/Mwani and 'certain dialects' use prosody grammatically) but says nothing about the catalog's Arabic-loan antepenultimate exceptions or syllabic nasals, so it neither supports nor contradicts those details.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Swahili (most dialects, Guthrie G41-43, Philippson's group XVIII) has lost all lexical and grammatical prosodic distinctions and has only a demarcative (non-contrastive) accent on the penultimate syllable of the word; it is the accentual end-point ('stade V') of the East Bantu tone-to-accent continuum. No dedicated Swahili chapter: Swahili is set aside from the analytic chapters precisely because it makes no distinctive use of prosody, and is cited as the pole of the typology and in the diachronic chapter.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Swahili (secondary accents are mentioned only generically, p. 44, as complicating the tone/accent typology).
new_statements.exceptions: Dialectal, not lexical: 'certains dialectes swahili' and the northern Swahili lects Mwiini (Chimwiini) and Mwani are classed '(a):1, (b):1, (c): oui' = no lexical tone but grammatical use of suprasegmentals; Mwiini keeps a weak penultimate vs final accent opposition in conjugation, nominals all penultimate (pp. 77-78, 422, 496-497). No mention of Arabic-loan antepenultimate stress in Standard Swahili.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's statements cover 'la plupart des parlers/dialectes swahili' (Guthrie G41-43, his group XVIII 'Sabaki') as a whole, i.e. Standard Swahili (Unguja-based) and most coastal dialects; he separates Mwiini (Chimwiini, Brava) and Mwani as northern/southern Swahili-group lects with residual grammatical accent, and Comorian (Ngazija, Ndzuani, Mwali) as tonal-accent systems. Ashton 1947 describes Standard (Zanzibar) Swahili; Contini-Morava 1997 Standard Swahili.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (StressTyp2 penultimate stress = fixed penultimate) and as Vitale 1982 in existing_statements, including the Arabic-loan exception; adds secondary stress in the verbal complex (penult from the right edge of the tense marker, after Barrett-Keach 1986), the rightward shift under suffixation, and notes the description is of Nairobi (non-standard) Swahili, where the same rule holds.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the penultimate syllable; adding a suffix (applicative -i-, locative -ni) moves stress rightward so it stays penultimate (ni-na-m-píg-a vs ni-na-m-pig-í-a; maktába vs maktabá-ni). The only exceptions are incompletely adapted loanwords, mainly Arabic, which may keep antepenultimate stress in free variation with the regular penultimate form (lázima ~ lazíma, héshima ~ heshíma); loans with original final stress are adapted by adding a final vowel so the stressed syllable becomes penultimate (kitábu, hiláli). The author interprets this as a trochaic-foot bias.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In the verbal complex, secondary stress falls on the subject-agreement marker or, with longer tense markers, on the penultimate syllable counted from the right edge of the tense marker (Nì-me-fíka, Ni-mèsha-fíka, Ni-mekwìsha-fíka), following Barrett-Keach (1986), who attributes it to a prosodic word boundary after T plus the ordinary penultimate rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (mostly Arabic) with antepenultimate stress in free variation with penultimate: lázima~lazíma, héshima~heshíma (citing Vitale 1985, 1992); Nairobi speakers shift between the standard lázima and colloquial lazíma; monosyllabic verb stems take dummy ku so a syllable is available to carry penultimate stress (sec. 2.4/2.6).
new_statements.identity_note: Deen 2002 describes Nairobi Swahili, a colloquial Kenyan variety the author places closer to the non-standard end of the continuum than to Kiswahili Sanifu (p. 17, fn. 18); the stress facts he reports (penultimate rule, loanword variation) are stated for Swahili generally and cited from standard-Swahili sources (Ashton 1947, Brandon 1975, Vitale 1985, Barrett-Keach 1986), with the Nairobi-specific remark that speakers shift between standard lázima and colloquial lazíma.

tone_statements.quote: In general, the next to last syllable of a Swahili word or phrase receives an accent, which consists of a slight increase in loudness, usually with some increase also in length. In those instances where the accent falls on some other syllable, its location is indicated in these materials by an acute accent: lázima [scanned: ldzima] 'necessary.' In Swahili, each vowel counts as a syllable, and in addition, pre-consonantal nasals are sometimes syllabic. These facts must be taken into account in calculating which syllable is the next-to-last. || Swahili, unlike other Bantu languages, is not a tone language. That is to say, there do not exist in the language pairs of words which are identical in their vowels and consonants, but different in musical pitch patterns and in meaning. Swahili does make use of a system of sentence intonation which is comparable to the intonation systems of Indo-European languages, although the details of Swahili sentence intonation are, of course, peculiar to Swahili. This aspect of the language has been discussed in some detail by Mrs. Ashton, and will not be described further here. || Note that in each word it is the next-to-last syllable that is accented.…

tone_statements.quote: Non-zero stress occurs on the penultimate syllabic of every utterance, and on various other syllabics (but never on two successive syllabics) within the utterance. We now break utterances into parts such that stress position is penultimate in each of these parts (such parts will turn out to be 'words' in the morphology). We do this by placing a juncture mark # immediately after the vowel following the stress vowel. Then, instead of writing ' over V when it occurs before ((C) C) V# (V representing the syllabics /a, e, i, o, u, m, n/), we now state that stress occurs automatically on the penultimate V in respect to #. Stress thus becomes dependent on a phonemic word juncture #.

sources.quote: In general, the next to last syllable of a Swahili word or phrase receives an accent, which consists of a slight increase in loudness, usually with some increase also in length. In those instances where the accent falls on some other syllable, its location is indicated in these materials by an acute accent: lázima [scanned: ldzima] 'necessary.' In Swahili, each vowel counts as a syllable, and in addition, pre-consonantal nasals are sometimes syllabic. These facts must be taken into account in calculating which syllable is the next-to-last. || Swahili, unlike other Bantu languages, is not a tone language. That is to say, there do not exist in the language pairs of words which are identical in their vowels and consonants, but different in musical pitch patterns and in meaning. Swahili does make use of a system of sentence intonation which is comparable to the intonation systems of Indo-European languages, although the details of Swahili sentence intonation are, of course, peculiar to Swahili. This aspect of the language has been discussed in some detail by Mrs. Ashton, and will not be described further here. || Note that in each word it is the next-to-last syllable that is accented.…
